docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This individual datasheet documents the design and development of the User Controls & Safety subsystem for Team 107's Simple Educational Robotic Arm.

The purpose of this subsystem is to provide user controls, monitor emergency-stop requests, and display operating status.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
Team 107 is developing a low-cost educational robotic arm capable of performing automated pick-and-place tasks.

The system consists of three subsystems:

  1. Arm Motion Control
  2. Gripper & Object Handling
  3. User Controls & Safety

Each subsystem uses a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller.

For additional project information, please visit the Team 107 Project Report.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
I am responsible for designing the User Controls & Safety subsystem.

The design includes:

  • Emergency Stop Monitoring
  • Start/Pause Control
  • Speed Control Potentiometer
  • Green and Red Status LEDs
  • ULN2003A Buzzer Driver
  • 5V Power Regulation
  • Team Communication Interface

The subsystem schematic was developed using KiCad and has passed the Electrical Rules Check (ERC).

This datasheet includes the block diagram, component selection, bill of materials, schematic design, power budget, and microcontroller configuration.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This block diagram describes the User Controls & Safety subsystem of the project.

The subsystem uses a Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano to process user inputs and provide system safety and status outputs.

The main user-control inputs include:

  • E-Stop Button
  • Start / Pause Button
  • Speed Knob (Potentiometer)

The main actuators and indicators include:

  • Green LED for run status
  • Red LED for fault or E-Stop indication
  • Buzzer for audible warning

The subsystem receives its required power from the project power distribution system and distributes the appropriate supply voltage to the microcontroller and user-interface components.

The subsystem communicates with other project subsystems through Connector 1 using digital and analog signals.

The primary inter-system signals include SAFE_OK, RUN_REQ, GRIP_CMD, OBJ_HELD, ARM_IN_POS, SPEED_SET, GRIP_FORCE, and GND.

docs.title: User Controls & Safety Subsystem
docs.text:
The User Controls & Safety subsystem provides the user interface for controlling the operation of the robotic system. This subsystem includes an emergency stop button, a start/pause button, a speed control input, status indicator LEDs, and an audible warning device.

The following component selections are based on the subsystem block diagram, electrical compatibility with the PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller, cost, PCB integration, and overall system requirements.

docs.title: 1. Speed Control Input Selection
docs.text:
The speed control input allows the operator to adjust the operating speed of the robotic system.

According to the current block diagram, the speed control device connects to the RA0/ANA0 analog input of the PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller.

Three potential solutions were evaluated.

Table 1: Speed Control Input Component Selection

Speed Control Input

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Bourns PTV09A-4015F-B10310k Ohm Linear Rotary Potentiometer$0.89/eachLink to ProductDatasheet • Provides a continuous analog voltage directly compatible with the PIC ADC input.• Inexpensive compared with the other options.• Compact design suitable for a user control panel.• Through-hole mounting simplifies PCB assembly. • Mechanical contact wear can introduce electrical noise over time.• Limited to approximately 280 degrees of rotation.• May require software filtering or calibration for stable speed adjustment. Option 2.Bourns PTA2043-2010DPB10310k Ohm Linear Slide Potentiometer$1.43/eachLink to ProductDatasheet • Provides a continuous analog voltage compatible with the PIC ADC input.• The slider position allows users to visually estimate the selected speed.• Linear resistance characteristics simplify the interpretation of speed settings.• Supports through-hole PCB mounting. • Requires more physical space than a rotary potentiometer.• More expensive than Option 1.• Sliding contacts may be affected by dust and mechanical wear.• Requires a different panel layout from the current speed knob design. Option 3.Bourns PEC11R-4215K-N002424 PPR Incremental Rotary Encoder$2.83/eachLink to ProductDatasheet • Supports continuous rotation without fixed mechanical end stops.• Digital signals allow adjustable speed increments through software.• Suitable for applications requiring step-by-step adjustment.• Through-hole mounting is available for PCB integration. • Requires two digital input channels instead of the existing analog input.• Requires additional software for quadrature decoding and debouncing.• More expensive than the other two solutions.• Would require modifications to the current block diagram and microcontroller pin assignments.

Choice: Option 1: Bourns PTV09A-4015F-B103 Linear Rotary Potentiometer.

Rationale: The Bourns PTV09A-4015F-B103 rotary potentiometer was selected because it provides a simple and reliable method for controlling the operating speed of the robotic system.

The selected component has a 10k Ohm resistance and a linear taper, allowing the microcontroller to interpret the potentiometer position through its analog-to-digital converter. This is compatible with the current subsystem block diagram, which assigns the speed control input to RA0/ANA0.

Compared with the slide potentiometer, the rotary potentiometer requires less panel space and provides an intuitive knob-based control interface. Compared with the rotary encoder, it requires fewer microcontroller input pins and does not need additional quadrature decoding software.

Furthermore, its through-hole mounting simplifies PCB integration, while its relatively low unit cost makes it suitable for the initial prototype.

Therefore, Option 1 provides the best balance of electrical compatibility, design simplicity, cost, and ease of integration for the User Controls & Safety subsystem.

docs.title: 2. Buzzer / Audio Alert Selection
docs.text:
The Buzzer / Audio Alert component is responsible for providing audible warnings when the robotic system encounters an emergency stop condition or an operating fault.

According to the subsystem block diagram, the buzzer is controlled by the PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller through the RB4 PWM output.

The selected buzzer should operate with the system's 5V power supply, provide sufficient sound output for laboratory use, and support programmable warning patterns.

Three potential solutions were evaluated.

Table 2: Buzzer / Audio Alert Component Selection

Buzzer / Audio Alert

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Same Sky CPT-1407-5THPassive Piezoelectric Buzzer5V, 5mA, 4kHz, 85dB$0.62/eachLink to Product • Compatible with externally generated PWM signals.• Low nominal current consumption of 5mA.• Inexpensive compared with the other options.• Through-hole mounting simplifies PCB assembly.• Supports programmable warning tones and alert patterns. • Requires an external oscillating signal to generate sound.• May require additional driver circuitry for reliable operation.• Sound output depends on the selected drive frequency and waveform.• Requires additional PWM configuration in software. Option 2.Same Sky CPI-137-83TActive Piezoelectric Buzzer5V, 10mA, 3.8kHz, 83dB$2.69/eachLink to Product • Contains an internal oscillator and does not require an external audio-frequency PWM signal.• Simple on/off control for warning applications.• Operates from the 5V power supply.• Through-hole mounting is suitable for PCB integration. • Higher cost than the passive piezoelectric buzzer.• Higher nominal current consumption than Option 1.• Fixed internal operating frequency limits tone customization.• Cannot directly use PWM frequency adjustment to generate different audio tones. Option 3.Same Sky CEM-1206SPassive Magnetic Buzzer5V, 45mA, 2.4kHz, 85dB$1.19/eachLink to Product • Supports externally generated audio-frequency signals.• Provides audible sound output suitable for warning applications.• Compact 12mm through-hole design.• Lower component cost than Option 2. • Higher nominal current consumption of 45mA.• Requires an external driver because of its current requirements.• Magnetic construction introduces inductive switching considerations.• Requires additional protection circuitry when driven by a switching transistor.

Choice: Option 1: Same Sky CPT-1407-5TH Passive Piezoelectric Buzzer.

Rationale: The CPT-1407-5TH passive piezoelectric buzzer was selected because it offers a suitable combination of PWM compatibility, low power consumption, compact size, and affordable cost for the User Controls & Safety subsystem.

The selected buzzer operates at a nominal voltage of 5V and has a specified operating frequency of 4kHz, making it suitable for use with a PWM signal generated by the PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller.

Compared with the active piezoelectric buzzer, Option 1 provides greater flexibility in generating different warning patterns and tones. Unlike the active buzzer, which contains its own oscillator, the passive buzzer allows the microcontroller to determine the frequency and timing of the warning signal.

Compared with the magnetic buzzer, Option 1 has significantly lower nominal current consumption, reducing the load on the subsystem's power supply.

Furthermore, its through-hole package simplifies PCB assembly and its 14mm diameter is suitable for integration into the user control board.

A suitable driver circuit will be evaluated during schematic design to ensure that the buzzer is driven within its electrical specifications.

Therefore, Option 1 provides the best overall balance of electrical compatibility, current consumption, cost, and controllability for the robotic system's audible warning function.

docs.title: 3. Buzzer Driver / Switching Device Selection
docs.text:
The buzzer driver is responsible for switching the audible warning device using a PWM control signal from the PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller.

The selected buzzer, Same Sky CPT-1407-5TH, is an externally driven piezoelectric transducer with a nominal current consumption of 5mA at its specified test conditions.

The driver should support the 5V buzzer supply, interface with the microcontroller's RB4 PWM signal, and be suitable for integration into the subsystem PCB.

Three switching devices were evaluated.

Table 3: Buzzer Driver / Switching Device Selection

Buzzer Driver / Switching Device

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.onsemi 2N3904TFNPN Bipolar Junction Transistor40V, 200mA, TO-92$0.29/eachLink to ProductDatasheet • Supports low-current switching applications.• Can be controlled using a 3.3V or 5V GPIO signal with an appropriate base resistor.• Through-hole TO-92 package simplifies PCB assembly and soldering.• Low component cost.• Easily interfaces with the existing PWM control signal. • Requires a base current during operation.• Requires an additional base resistor.• Has a collector-emitter saturation voltage when switched on.• Not as power-efficient as a suitable MOSFET for higher-current applications. Option 2.Diotec Semiconductor 2N7000N-Channel MOSFET60V, 200mA, TO-92$0.29/eachLink to ProductDatasheet • Voltage-controlled gate requires very little steady-state current.• Through-hole mounting simplifies manual PCB assembly.• Suitable for low-current switching applications.• Low cost compared with other driver solutions. • Low on-resistance is specified at higher gate-drive voltages, not guaranteed at 3.3V.• Switching performance must be verified with the actual GPIO voltage.• Requires a gate pull-down resistor for reliable startup behavior.• Provides no significant functional advantage over the NPN transistor for this low-current buzzer. Option 3.Alpha & Omega AO3400ALogic-Level N-Channel MOSFET30V, 5.7A rated, SOT-23$0.52/eachLink to ProductDatasheet • Low on-resistance, including at a 2.5V gate-drive voltage.• Compatible with low-voltage microcontroller control signals.• Requires very little steady-state gate current.• Suitable for PWM switching applications.• Compact PCB footprint. • Small SOT-23 surface-mount package requires more careful soldering.• Higher price than Options 1 and 2.• Current capability is much greater than needed for the selected buzzer.• Requires a gate pull-down resistor to prevent unintended switching during startup.

Final Choice (Revised): ULN2003A Darlington Transistor Array.

Rationale: Following the schematic design review, the original 2N3904 transistor-based buzzer driver was replaced with the ULN2003A Darlington transistor array.

The updated design uses the PIC18F57Q43 RC4 pin (PWM1OUT1) to generate a 4 kHz PWM signal for the buzzer-control circuit. The ULN2003A provides a low-side switching interface between the microcontroller and the externally powered 5 V buzzer.

The selected Same Sky CPT-1407-5TH passive piezoelectric buzzer remains unchanged.

The ULN2003A was selected for the revised design because it provides an integrated transistor-driver solution with internal input resistors and multiple available driver channels.

The PWM output is initially configured with a 0% duty cycle. The application firmware will control the buzzer during warning conditions.

This revision supersedes the original 2N3904 driver selection. Final electrical operation will be verified during hardware testing.

docs.title: 4. Power Source and Voltage Regulation Selection
docs.text:
The User Controls & Safety subsystem uses two separate power sources. The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano and its associated user interface components operate from USB power, while a 9V external DC adapter and a 5V linear regulator supply the external buzzer circuit.

According to the EGR304 project requirements, each individual subsystem must include a 5V linear voltage regulator and a barrel jack connection for a 9V external power supply.

The power system must provide stable voltage regulation, sufficient current capacity, and safe operating conditions for all connected components.

docs.title: 4.1 Linear Voltage Regulator Selection
docs.text:
Three 5V linear voltage regulators were evaluated based on electrical characteristics, current capacity, cost, and PCB integration.

Table 4: Linear Voltage Regulator Selection

5V Linear Voltage Regulator

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.STMicroelectronics L7805CV5V Fixed Linear Regulator1.5A, TO-220$1.08/eachLink to ProductDatasheet • Provides a regulated 5V output compatible with the subsystem.• Supports a 9V DC input supply.• Rated for up to 1.5A with appropriate thermal management.• Inexpensive compared with the other options.• Through-hole TO-220 package simplifies PCB assembly.• Includes thermal shutdown and short-circuit protection. • Generates heat because the excess input voltage is dissipated as power loss.• May require a heatsink at higher load currents.• Requires appropriate input and output capacitors.• Higher dropout voltage compared with an LDO regulator. Option 2.STMicroelectronics L78M05CV5V Fixed Linear Regulator500mA, TO-220$1.16/eachLink to ProductDatasheet • Provides a regulated 5V output compatible with the subsystem.• Supports a 9V input supply.• Suitable for low-current electronic systems.• Through-hole mounting simplifies PCB integration.• Includes internal protection against overheating and short circuits. • Lower rated current capacity of 500mA.• Provides less current headroom for additional peripheral devices.• Still dissipates excess voltage as heat.• Slightly higher unit cost than Option 1. Option 3.STMicroelectronics L4940V55V Low-Dropout Linear Regulator1.5A, TO-220$2.68/eachLink to ProductDatasheet • Provides a stable regulated 5V output.• Low dropout voltage supports operation with input voltages closer to 5V.• Rated for up to 1.5A with adequate thermal management.• Through-hole TO-220 package is suitable for PCB assembly.• Includes thermal and short-circuit protection. • More expensive than the other two solutions.• Low-dropout capability offers limited benefit with the specified 9V supply.• Still requires thermal management when reducing 9V to 5V.• Requires appropriate input and output capacitors, including attention to output capacitor stability requirements.

Choice: Option 1: STMicroelectronics L7805CV Linear Voltage Regulator.

Rationale: The STMicroelectronics L7805CV was selected because it provides a cost-effective and straightforward method for converting the required 9V input supply into a regulated 5V output.

The selected regulator provides a fixed 5V output and has a rated current capacity of up to 1.5A, subject to appropriate thermal management.

In the current design, the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano is powered separately through USB, while the L7805CV supplies the external buzzer circuit and its proposed minimum-load resistor.

This arrangement provides regulated power for the externally powered components while keeping the microcontroller's USB supply separate from the external 5V power rail.

Compared with the L78M05CV, the L7805CV provides a higher rated output current at a slightly lower unit cost.

Compared with the L4940V5, the L7805CV offers a simpler and less expensive solution for the required 9V input. Since the subsystem uses a nominal 9V supply, the lower dropout voltage of the L4940V5 is not a significant advantage.

The TO-220 through-hole package also simplifies manual soldering, PCB integration, and possible heatsink installation.

Although linear regulation produces heat, the selected regulator is suitable for the proposed design provided that the final power budget and thermal calculations confirm safe operating conditions.

Therefore, Option 1 provides an appropriate balance of electrical compatibility, current capacity, cost, and PCB assembly requirements.

docs.title: 4.2 External 9V Power Source Selection
docs.text:
The external power source must supply 9V DC to the subsystem through a barrel jack connector.

Three commercially available AC/DC power adapters were evaluated based on voltage regulation, maximum current, connector compatibility, and cost.

Table 5: External Power Source Selection

9V External Power Supply

Solution Pros Cons Option 1.Jameco ReliaPro DCU090050RZ74809V DC Wall Adapter500mA, 4.5W$10.53/eachLink to Product • Provides the required 9V DC output.• Uses a center-positive 5.5mm/2.1mm barrel connector.• Suitable for low-current subsystem applications.• Compact wall-mounted power source. • Limited to a maximum output current of 500mA.• Provides less current headroom than the other options.• Designed for 120V AC input rather than universal AC input.• Requires verification that the final power budget fits within its current rating. Option 2.Pololu 14709V DC Wall Adapter1A, 9W$11.41/eachLink to Product • Provides the required 9V DC output.• Supports a maximum output current of 1A.• Compatible with 100–240V AC input.• Uses a center-positive 5.5mm/2.1mm barrel connector.• Provides sufficient current headroom for a moderate-load subsystem. • Higher unit cost than the other two options.• Lower current capacity than Option 3.• Requires an external AC outlet.• Connector fit and final load requirements must still be verified. Option 3.Tensility International 16-001349V DC Wall Adapter2A, 18W$10.53/eachLink to Product • Provides the required regulated 9V DC output.• Supports a maximum output current of 2A.• Compatible with 100–240V AC input.• Uses a center-positive 5.5mm/2.1mm barrel connector.• Provides additional source current headroom for future design changes. • Higher current capacity than the present subsystem may require.• Requires an external AC outlet and reduces portability.• Must be connected to a barrel jack with matching dimensions and polarity.• Additional adapter current capacity does not eliminate the linear regulator's thermal limitations.

Choice: Option 3: Tensility International 16-00134 9V DC Wall Adapter.

Rationale: The Tensility International 16-00134 was provisionally selected because it provides the required 9V DC output with sufficient current capacity for the proposed power distribution system.

The adapter supports up to 2A of output current and operates from a 100–240V AC input. Its center-positive 5.5mm/2.1mm barrel connector is suitable for integration with a compatible PCB-mounted barrel jack.

Compared with the Jameco 500mA adapter, Option 3 provides greater current headroom for possible future changes to the subsystem.

Compared with the Pololu 1A adapter, Option 3 offers a higher rated current capacity at a similar or lower unit cost.

The higher current rating does not mean that the subsystem will continuously draw 2A. Actual current consumption depends on the connected components, while the linear regulator's safe output current will also depend on thermal conditions.

Therefore, Option 3 provides a practical external power source for the subsystem. The final selection will be confirmed after completing the power budget, verifying the barrel jack dimensions, and calculating regulator power dissipation.

docs.title: 5.1 Microcontroller Information
docs.text:
The User Controls & Safety subsystem uses the Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano development board as the main controller.

The microcontroller is responsible for reading user inputs, controlling status indicators, generating PWM signals for the audible warning system, and communicating with other subsystems through the team connector.

The microcontroller is powered through USB, while the external buzzer circuit is powered by a separate 5V linear voltage regulator.

Table 6: Microcontroller Information

Parameter Description Manufacturer Microchip Technology Microcontroller PIC18F57Q43 Development Board PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano Target Voltage 5V Clock Source HFINTOSC System Clock 64 MHz Clock Divider 1 Power Source USB Digital Interfaces GPIO and PWM Analog Interfaces ADC and DAC Subsystem User Controls & Safety

docs.title: 5.2 Microcontroller Pin Assignment
docs.text:
The following table summarizes the proposed microcontroller pin assignments based on the individual block diagram.

Table 7: PIC18F57Q43 Pin Assignment

PIC Pin Signal Name Direction Function RB0 E_STOP Digital Input Emergency stop button RB1 START_PAUSE Digital Input Start/Pause button RA0/ANA0 SPEED_KNOB Analog Input Speed control potentiometer RB2 GREEN_LED Digital Output Normal operation indicator RB3 RED_LED Digital Output Fault/Emergency stop indicator RB4 BUZZER_PWM PWM Output Audible warning control RD0 SAFE_OK Digital Output Safety status signal RD1 RUN_REQ Digital Output System run request RD2 GRIP_CMD Digital Output Gripper control command RD3 OBJ_HELD Digital Input Object detection feedback RD4 ARM_IN_POS Digital Input Arm position feedback RA2/DAC1 SPEED_SET Analog Output Speed command to other subsystems RA1/ANA1 GRIP_FORCE Analog Input Gripper force feedback

These assignments are based on the current individual block diagram. The final physical pin connections and peripheral configurations will be verified during schematic design and MPLAB Code Configurator setup.

docs.title: 5.3 Team Connector Pin Assignment
docs.text:
The User Controls & Safety subsystem communicates with other team subsystems through an 8-pin connector.

The connector includes digital control signals, analog signals, and a common ground connection.

Table 8: Team Connector Pin Assignment

Connector Pin Signal Name PIC Pin Direction Signal Type 1 SAFE_OK RD0 Output Digital 2 RUN_REQ RD1 Output Digital 3 GRIP_CMD RD2 Output Digital 4 OBJ_HELD RD3 Input Digital 5 ARM_IN_POS RD4 Input Digital 6 SPEED_SET RA2/DAC1 Output Analog 7 GRIP_FORCE RA1/ANA1 Input Analog 8 GND System GND Ground Ground

The connector assignments follow the current subsystem block diagram and will be confirmed with the team before final PCB design.

The connector ground provides a common reference for digital and analog communication between the subsystems.

docs.title: 5.4 Design Considerations
docs.text:
The final PCB and firmware design must verify the following:

  • Digital input pins are configured with appropriate pull-up or pull-down resistors.
  • Analog input signals remain within the microcontroller's permitted voltage range.
  • PWM output is correctly configured through the microcontroller's peripheral pin selection system.
  • The selected buzzer driver supports the required load and control signal.
  • The USB-powered microcontroller and externally powered buzzer circuit share a common ground without directly connecting their separate 5V supply outputs.
  • The emergency stop function is evaluated for the required safety behavior. A software-only emergency stop signal must not be treated as a guaranteed hardware power-disconnection mechanism.
  • Team connector signal directions and physical pin numbering are confirmed before PCB fabrication.

The final pin assignments will be validated during hardware integration and testing.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic describes the User Controls and Safety Subsystem of our robotic system. The subsystem uses a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano microcontroller to process user inputs, monitor emergency-stop requests, control status indicators, generate audible alerts, and communicate with other robotic subsystems.

The main functional blocks include power regulation, emergency-stop monitoring, start/pause control, speed adjustment, LED indicators, a ULN2003A buzzer driver, communication interfaces, and debugging and expansion features.

The schematic has been reorganized using descriptive net labels to improve readability, simplify signal tracing, and reduce unnecessary wiring across the drawing.

docs.title: Complete Schematic — Revision C
docs.text:
Figure 1: Revised schematic of the User Controls and Safety Subsystem, including the updated buzzer driver and reorganized signal connections.

View High-Resolution Schematic

docs.title: 1. Power Regulation
docs.text:
The circuit receives an external 9–12 V DC supply through J1, a barrel jack connector.

F1 provides overcurrent protection, while U2, an L7805 linear voltage regulator, generates the regulated +5V_EXT supply rail.

C1, C2, and C3 provide input and output filtering to improve voltage stability.

The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano is powered through its USB connection, while the external circuitry uses the regulated +5V_EXT supply. The two circuits share a common ground reference.

The final fuse rating, regulator thermal performance, and power consumption will be verified during hardware implementation.

docs.title: 2. Microcontroller
docs.text:
The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano serves as the main controller for the subsystem.

It reads user inputs through digital GPIO and ADC connections, generates control outputs, operates status indicators, and communicates with other robotic subsystems.

A custom KiCad symbol and footprint were created for the Curiosity Nano development board.

Descriptive net labels connect the microcontroller to the other functional blocks, improving the organization and readability of the schematic.

docs.title: 3. Emergency-Stop Monitoring
docs.text:
SW1 is a normally closed emergency-stop switch.

R1 provides a pull-up resistor, while C5 provides input filtering.

Under normal conditions, the switch holds the E_STOP signal LOW. When the switch opens, the signal is pulled HIGH.

The E_STOP signal is connected to RB0 of the microcontroller, allowing the firmware to detect a stop request.

J6 provides an external connection for the physical emergency-stop switch.

This circuit provides stop-request monitoring but does not replace an independent, safety-rated hardware shutdown system.

docs.title: 4. Start/Pause and Speed Control
docs.text:
SW2 provides the start/pause input.

R2 and C4 form a pull-up and RC filtering circuit for the START_PAUSE signal, which is connected to RB1.

RV1 is a 10 kΩ potentiometer used to adjust the requested operating speed.

The potentiometer generates an adjustable analog voltage. R3 and C7 provide filtering before the POT_ADC signal reaches RA0, which is configured as an ADC input.

The microcontroller processes the analog speed request and can generate a corresponding speed command through RA2 using the SPEED_SET signal.

POT_ADC and SPEED_SET are separate signals: POT_ADC represents the user's speed adjustment input, while SPEED_SET provides the speed command to the connected subsystem.

docs.title: 5. Status Indicators
docs.text:
Green and red LEDs provide visual indications of system operating conditions.

Each LED includes a current-limiting resistor to prevent excessive current.

The green LED is controlled through RB2, while the red LED is controlled through RB3.

An additional debug LED is connected through RF2 to support circuit testing and troubleshooting.

docs.title: 6. ULN2003A Buzzer Driver
docs.text:
The original buzzer circuit used an individual 2N3904 transistor. Following instructor feedback, the circuit was updated to use a ULN2003A Darlington driver IC.

The microcontroller generates the BUZZER_ENABLE control signal through RC4.

JP1 provides a connection between the control signal and the first input channel of U3.

The corresponding ULN2003A output channel provides low-side switching for the buzzer.

The input circuitry includes a pull-down resistor to establish a defined logic state when the control signal is disconnected.

Unused input channels are also connected to a defined LOW state.

The final buzzer drive method, operating voltage, and audible output will be verified against the selected component's datasheet during hardware testing.

docs.title: 7. Team Communication
docs.text:
J2 provides an eight-pin interface for communication with the other robotic subsystems.

The interface includes the following signals:

SAFE_OK

RUN_REQ

GRIP_CMD

OBJ_HELD

ARM_IN_POS

SPEED_SET

GRIP_FORCE

GND

The SPEED_SET signal is generated through the microcontroller's RA2 output, while GRIP_FORCE is connected to RA1 for analog measurement.

J3 and J4 provide additional UART communication interfaces using the microcontroller's RC3 and RC2 connections.

These connectors allow the user-control subsystem to exchange operating commands and status information with the other subsystems.

docs.title: 8. Debugging and Expansion
docs.text:
SW3 provides an additional debugging input through the DEBUG_SW signal, connected to RE0.

The debug input includes a pull-up resistor and an RC filtering capacitor.

J5 provides access to the external 5 V supply, ground, and spare GPIO connections for future expansion.

Test points are included at selected circuit nodes to support voltage measurements, debugging, and signal verification during hardware testing.

These features improve the flexibility and maintainability of the subsystem during development.

docs.title: Design Revision
docs.text:
Revision A: Initial schematic using a 2N3904 transistor for buzzer switching.

Revision B: Updated buzzer driver using a ULN2003A driver IC in response to instructor feedback.

Revision C: Reorganized the schematic using descriptive net labels, separated functional circuit blocks, and clarified microcontroller signal connections to improve readability and maintainability.

The revised schematic has passed KiCad Electrical Rules Check (ERC).

Physical testing, final component verification, and system-level validation remain part of the hardware implementation process.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The purpose of this power budget is to evaluate the electrical power requirements of the User Controls & Safety subsystem.

This subsystem includes a PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller, emergency stop and start/pause buttons, a speed control potentiometer, status indicator LEDs, and an audible warning buzzer.

According to the project requirements, the subsystem uses a 9V external DC power supply and a 5V linear voltage regulator.

The power budget will be used to estimate the maximum current consumption of each component, determine the total power requirements, and verify that the selected voltage regulator and external power supply can safely support the subsystem.

The calculations will also include a 25% current safety margin and an evaluation of the voltage regulator's power dissipation.
